newsitem.title: USA: Alabama Power, commission sued over electric law.
newsitem.headline: Alabama Power, commission sued over electric law.

text.p: Southern Company's Alabama Power and three Alabama Public Service Commissioners were sued Monday by a power marketer and two consumer groups over a law that limited consumers' incentive to switch away from the local utility to buy power from other suppliers.

The law, passed by the Alabama legislature last year, guaranteed that Alabama Power would be able to recoup from departing customers the costs of assets that the utility said would become uneconomic when the retail or wholesale customers stopped buying power from it.

The lawsuit was filed by American Energy Solutions, the Alabama Electric Consumers Coalition, and the conservative Citizens for a Sound Economy against the utility and the commissioners to block the law from being implemented.

"The last thing we would want is a monopoly within the state making a decision on what's good for you and I as a customer," said Greg Elam, president of American Energy Solutions, which arranges energy supplies and manages price risk for customers such as municipal utilities and industries.
The groups said the Alabama law was unconstitutional because it restrained interstate trade in electric power.

"The effect of the law is to create an impenetrable wall around Alabama consumers, preventing them from attempting to buy electricity from suppliers in other states who may offer cheaper rates," according to a summary of the lawsuit.

American Energy Solutions, an energy marketer, said it had identified potential customers in Alabama, but added that any savings it could provide them would be eliminated if Alabama Power was allowed to set and collect stranded costs from them.

The groups also said the state law preempted a federal law, the Public Utilities Regulatory Policies Act, by restricting the ability of small power producers and cogenerators to find new buyers, and usurped the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which has jurisdiction over all wholesale electricity markets.
Alabama has not introduced retail competition, but lawmakers are expected to reintroduce a bill, which stalled last year, to let consumers choose their power suppliers.
Southern Company officials were not immediately available for comment.
